desiccated-thyroid-armour.summary: Dried porcine thyroid supplying T4 and T3; people use it hoping a faster metabolism helps them get leaner.

quick.overview:
Desiccated thyroid is dried animal thyroid gland that supplies both T4 and T3 hormone. People who talk about it for looks are after a faster metabolism, lower body fat and a leaner look. Armour Thyroid is the best-known brand.

The chain runs through thyroid hormone receptors: added T4 and T3 raise metabolic rate, which in theory means more energy burned. It is an older hypothyroidism treatment, and excessive thyroid hormone does cause weight loss in medical settings, but no study has tested it as a slimming treatment in people with normal thyroid function.
quick.how: It is a prescription treatment for an underactive thyroid, taken by mouth. Some people with normal thyroid function discuss adding it to a diet and training plan to support fat loss. Medical use is monitored with blood tests, and guidelines generally prefer synthetic levothyroxine for hypothyroidism.
quick.risks: Excess thyroid hormone can cause fast or irregular heartbeat, anxiety, fever and, at worst, heart failure. Batch variability and high T3 peaks are cited concerns. It is prescription-only and is not indicated for weight loss.

angle.text: Desiccated thyroid supplies T4 and T3, and people use it hoping the extra hormone raises metabolic rate and helps them carry less body fat. It is an older hypothyroidism treatment; no trials have tested it for slimming.

medroxyprogesterone-acetate.summary: A prescription progestin (Depo-Provera) used in feminizing hormone therapy and for hirsutism, where it shifts hormone balance and hair growth.

quick.overview:
Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) is a synthetic progestin best known as a contraceptive. For appearance, it is used in feminizing hormone regimens for transgender women and to treat excess body and facial hair (hirsutism), and decreased scalp hair is a listed side effect.

It activates progesterone, androgen and glucocorticoid receptors and suppresses GnRH, which lowers sex hormone levels and shifts the hormone balance behind body shape and hair growth. High-dose injectable MPA has been reported to treat hirsutism; trial data for its appearance uses are limited.
quick.how: MPA comes as an oral tablet and as an injectable contraceptive (Depo-Provera), prescribed by a clinician. In feminizing therapy it is added to an estrogen-based regimen at a prescriber's discretion. Results on hair or body shape build over months.
quick.risks: The injectable label carries a boxed warning for loss of bone mineral density. Blood clots, menstrual disruption and meningioma have been reported, and large trials of estrogen plus MPA in postmenopausal women found higher rates of breast cancer, coronary disease and stroke. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Medroxyprogesterone acetate is used in feminizing hormone therapy and for hirsutism, where progestin activity shifts hormone balance, body shape and hair growth. These are off-label to its contraceptive role, with limited trial data for them.

megestrol-acetate.summary: A prescription progestin appetite stimulant used in cancer and AIDS wasting; people interested in gaining weight on a thin frame discuss it for the appetite boost.

quick.overview:
Megestrol acetate is a prescription progestin approved for advanced breast and endometrial cancer and for anorexia or wasting in people with AIDS. For looks, it comes up with people who want a fuller body and want to eat more than they can manage on their own.

The chain is appetite, then more calories, then weight gain. Published weight-gain results come from sick populations such as people with cancer or HIV; reviews describe limited evidence in elderly patients, and no trials have tested it in healthy people seeking cosmetic weight gain.
quick.how: It is a prescription medicine taken by mouth, usually as an oral suspension in medical use. In physique discussions it is considered alongside calorie-dense eating plans and training. Appetite changes are the effect people look for.
quick.risks: Documented risks include fluid retention, blood clots, adrenal suppression, lowered sex hormones, bone loss and fetal harm; it is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is prescription-only in the US and most countries, and the maker of its branded suspension settled a 2013 lawsuit over off-label promotion.

angle.text: Megestrol is a progestin appetite stimulant that people considering weight gain on a thin frame discuss: more appetite means more calories, which means a fuller body. Its weight-gain effect is documented in cancer and AIDS wasting; cosmetic use has not been studied.

cyproheptadine.summary: An allergy antihistamine that increases appetite; used off-label for weight gain in children and discussed by people trying to eat more while bulking.

quick.overview:
Cyproheptadine is an older antihistamine approved for allergies. It also blocks serotonin receptors, which raises appetite, and people who want to gain weight or bulk use it to eat more.

The chain is more appetite, higher calorie intake, then weight gain and more mass. Increased appetite and weight gain are recognised effects, and doctors prescribe it off-label for underweight children. No trial has tested it in healthy adults for cosmetic or bodybuilding goals.
quick.how: It comes as a tablet or syrup. In bulking discussions it is taken to make larger meals easier, and some forum posts mention combining it with other supplements. Appetite changes tend to appear within days to weeks.
quick.risks: Common effects are drowsiness, dizziness and dry mouth, plus other anticholinergic effects such as urinary retention. Rare liver and blood problems are reported, and overdose in children can cause convulsions and death. It is prescription-only in the US and Canada and over the counter in the UK.

angle.text: Cyproheptadine is an antihistamine that raises appetite, so people use it to eat more while bulking or gaining weight. Appetite gain is documented, mainly in children; cosmetic weight gain has not been studied.

methylphenidate.summary: An ADHD stimulant whose appetite suppression leads some people to use it to eat less and lean out.

quick.overview:
Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) is a prescription stimulant for ADHD and narcolepsy. Reduced appetite and weight loss are among its most common effects, so people who want to lean out discuss it as a way to eat less while staying focused.

The chain is lower appetite, fewer calories eaten, then fat loss. Its weight effects are documented as side effects in ADHD patients; it has not been tested as a weight-loss or cosmetic treatment in healthy people.
quick.how: It is prescribed as short- or extended-release tablets or capsules, usually taken in the morning. People who discuss it for leaning out pair it with calorie tracking and training. Appetite suppression is noticeable soon after dosing.
quick.risks: The US label carries a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction. Other documented effects include insomnia, anxiety, raised heart rate and blood pressure, rare psychiatric events and reduced growth in children. It is Schedule II in the US and Class B in the UK.

angle.text: Methylphenidate suppresses appetite, so people use it to eat less and get leaner, often alongside its focus effect. It is an ADHD stimulant; weight loss is a documented side effect and has not been tested as a goal.

amphetamine-adderall.summary: A prescription stimulant that suppresses appetite; looksmaxxing forum users discuss it for eating less and leaning out.

quick.overview:
Adderall is a prescription mixed-amphetamine product for ADHD and narcolepsy. Forum users discuss it for appetite control and leaning out, and some also report more social ease and gym drive.

The chain is less appetite, fewer calories, then fat loss. Appetite loss and weight loss are common documented effects, and amphetamines are listed among appetite suppressants, but no trial has tested Adderall as a weight-loss or appearance treatment in healthy people.
quick.how: It is prescribed as immediate- or extended-release tablets or capsules. Those who use it for appearance pair appetite control with calorie tracking and gym work. Non-medical use is common among US college students, and forum users note that unprescribed pills may not be what they claim.
quick.risks: Documented effects include higher heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, anxiety, psychosis at heavy use, and dependence with withdrawal. It is Schedule II in the US, Class B in the UK and Schedule I in Canada. Unprescribed pills may contain other substances.

angle.text: Adderall suppresses appetite, so some people use it to eat less and lean out, and report more focus and gym drive. Appetite suppression is a documented effect; weight loss and looks were not what it was studied for.

lisdexamfetamine-vyvanse.summary: A dextroamphetamine prodrug approved for ADHD and binge-eating disorder; people discuss it for its appetite-reducing effect when trying to lean out.

quick.overview:
Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse in the US, Elvanse in Europe) is a prescription stimulant approved for ADHD and for moderate to severe binge-eating disorder (BED) in adults. For looks, people interested in leaning out cite its appetite-reducing effect.

The drug is inactive until red blood cells release dextroamphetamine, which raises norepinephrine and dopamine signalling and reduces appetite. Trials in BED measured binge-eating days, not body weight as a cosmetic goal, and the US label states it is not indicated for weight loss.
quick.how: It is prescribed as a once-daily capsule or chewable tablet. Its gradual release makes it a smoother option than immediate-release amphetamine for some people. Appetite effects appear soon after starting.
quick.risks: It is a Schedule II controlled substance in the US with a boxed warning for abuse, misuse and addiction. The label also warns of cardiovascular risks, raised blood pressure and heart rate, and psychiatric reactions such as mania or psychosis, and it is contraindicated with MAO inhibitors. It requires a prescription.

angle.text: Vyvanse is discussed for its appetite-reducing effect: eating less leads to weight loss and a leaner look. It is approved for ADHD and binge-eating disorder; weight loss for appearance has not been the studied purpose.

quinine-skin-bleaching.summary: Quinine appears in reports of unregulated skin-lightening products where users wanted a lighter complexion; no research describes it as a lightener.

quick.overview:
Quinine is a bitter alkaloid from cinchona bark, best known as an antimalarial and as a flavouring in tonic water. For looks, it appears in reports of unregulated skin-lightening products that people used to get a lighter complexion; in a 1997 Paris trafficking case, some users turned to products containing corticosteroids or quinine alongside mercury- or bleach-based preparations.

No lightening mechanism is described. No clinical studies of quinine for skin lightening were found, and its established action is against malaria parasites.
quick.how: Quinine reaches this use only as an ingredient reported in illicit lightening products, not as a cosmetic with a defined routine. Regulated skin-lightening options are a separate category.
quick.risks: Quinine at therapeutic levels can cause cinchonism (ringing in the ears, headache, nausea, vision changes) and, rarely, serious blood and heart-rhythm problems. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia. Unregulated lightening products have been reported to contain other hazardous agents such as mercury and potent steroids.

angle.text: Quinine appears in reports of unregulated skin-lightening products, where users sought a lighter overall complexion. It is an antimalarial and tonic-water flavouring; no studies of it as a lightener were found.

ascorbyl-glucoside.summary: A stabilised vitamin C derivative in serums and creams that brightens skin, evens tone and softens signs of ageing.

quick.overview:
Ascorbyl glucoside is vitamin C with a glucose unit attached, which keeps it stable in skincare formulas. People use it in serums and creams for brighter skin, more even tone and fewer visible pigment marks.

It is described as a precursor that releases ascorbic acid in the skin, where vitamin C acts as an antioxidant and reduces melanin production. A small case series used an ascorbyl glucoside preparation with iontophoresis in melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and it appears among whitening ingredients in cosmetic analysis papers; its rate of conversion to ascorbic acid is unknown.
quick.how: It is applied daily as a leave-on serum or cream, often in the morning under sunscreen and paired with other brightening ingredients such as niacinamide. Skincare communities treat it as a gentler, more stable alternative to pure ascorbic acid. Visible brightening is typically judged over weeks.
quick.risks: No specific safety problems are described in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, and like any topical it can be tolerated differently from person to person.

angle.text: Ascorbyl glucoside is a stabilised vitamin C derivative used in serums to brighten skin, even tone and slow visible ageing, by delivering antioxidant vitamin C and reducing melanin production. Research specific to this derivative is small.

cetyl-tranexamate-mesylate.summary: A fat-soluble form of tranexamic acid used in serums to fade dark spots and even skin tone.

quick.overview:
Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a modified form of tranexamic acid made for skincare. People use it in serums aimed at dark spots, uneven tone and post-acne marks.

Tranexamic acid is thought to reduce the signalling that drives melanocyte pigment production, and the cetyl chain makes the molecule more fat-soluble so it can cross the skin barrier better than the parent compound. A 2021 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology examined its skin-lightening performance on sun-damaged skin, and a small registered trial looked at acne-related hyperpigmentation.
quick.how: It is applied as a leave-on serum or cream, usually daily and often with sunscreen, since sun exposure drives pigmentation. It is commonly combined with other brightening ingredients. Fading of marks is judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Sources reviewed report no specific safety concerns, but long-term data are lacking. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient; as with any topical, irritation is possible.

angle.text: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a fat-soluble tranexamic acid form used in serums to reduce pigment production, so dark spots fade and tone looks more even. Published data include a 2021 cosmetic-dermatology study and a small registered trial.

piroctone-olamine.summary: An antifungal shampoo ingredient that clears dandruff and flaking so your scalp and hair look cleaner.

quick.overview:
Piroctone olamine is an antifungal ingredient in many anti-dandruff shampoos. People use it to clear flakes and itch and keep the scalp healthy, so hair looks cleaner.

It targets the Malassezia yeasts linked to flaking. It is thought to enter fungal cells and bind iron, disrupting energy production, though the exact mechanism is not fully established. Studies have compared it with zinc pyrithione and ketoconazole shampoos for dandruff and shedding; it is a scalp-condition ingredient rather than a hair-growth treatment.
quick.how: It is used as a regular wash-in shampoo, lathered on the scalp and rinsed, often a few times a week. It is sold under names such as Octopirox in cosmetic formulations. Flaking typically eases over a few weeks of regular use.
quick.risks: EU rules cap it at 1.0% in rinse-off and 0.5% in other cosmetics. Labels advise avoiding the eyes and stopping use if irritation or allergy occurs.

angle.text: Piroctone olamine is an anti-dandruff shampoo ingredient that acts on scalp yeasts, clearing flakes and itch so the scalp and hair look cleaner. Trials have compared it with zinc pyrithione for dandruff; hair growth is not its documented use.

zinc-pyrithione.summary: The classic dandruff-shampoo antifungal that clears flakes and calms scalp irritation for cleaner-looking hair.

quick.overview:
Zinc pyrithione is the active in many dandruff shampoos and body washes. People use it to clear flakes and scalp itch and manage seborrheic dermatitis, which leaves the scalp and hair looking cleaner.

It acts against the yeasts linked to flaking, thought to work by disrupting fungal membrane transport and raising intracellular copper, which damages iron-sulfur proteins. It has been used in dandruff products for decades, is approved as an over-the-counter dandruff ingredient in the US and is a standard comparator in dandruff trials. It is not a hair-growth treatment.
quick.how: It is used as a regular shampoo, lathered on the scalp, left for a few minutes and rinsed, commonly a few times a week. Many people rotate it with other anti-dandruff actives. Flaking usually improves within a few weeks.
quick.risks: US labels warn against use on damaged skin or in young children. The EU classifies it as a reproductive toxicant and has barred it in cosmetics since December 2021; it is also toxic to aquatic life as an antifouling agent.

angle.text: Zinc pyrithione is the classic dandruff-shampoo active; it clears flakes and calms scalp irritation so the scalp and hair look cleaner. It is well studied for dandruff and is not promoted for hair growth.

selenium-disulfide.summary: An old-school dandruff shampoo active (Selsun Blue) that clears flakes and scalp scaling for a cleaner look.

quick.overview:
Selenium disulfide is an antifungal and keratolytic ingredient in dandruff shampoos such as Selsun Blue. People use it to clear dandruff and scalp scaling, so the scalp and hair look cleaner; it is also used for scalp seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor.

It acts against Malassezia yeast and loosens scale as a keratolytic, though its detailed molecular mechanism is not well described. It entered US medical use in 1951 and is on the WHO Essential Medicines List. For seborrheic dermatitis it is generally tried after ketoconazole.
quick.how: It is used as a medicated shampoo, lathered on the scalp, left for a few minutes and rinsed, usually a couple of times a week at first. The best-known over-the-counter product is Selsun Blue (1% selenium disulfide). Strength limits differ by country.
quick.risks: Scalp itching, burning, hair lightening, orange staining and discolouration of jewellery are reported. Absorption is higher through damaged skin, and labels advise avoiding it there.

angle.text: Selenium disulfide shampoos such as Selsun Blue clear dandruff and scalp scaling, so the scalp looks cleaner and hair looks tidier. It is used for scalp conditions; hair growth is not its documented use.

erythrulose.summary: A raspberry-derived sugar used with DHA in self-tanners to build a gradual, bronze-toned sunless tan.

quick.overview:
Erythrulose is a small sugar found in fruits such as raspberries and used in sunless tanning products, usually together with DHA. It gives a bronzed look without sun exposure, with colour that shows within hours.

It reacts with amino acids in the outer skin layer in a Maillard-type reaction to form brown pigments, more slowly than DHA. Cosmetic-industry descriptions say combining the two affects colour development and evenness, with a more gradual build and more even fade; no clinical trials of its tanning performance were found.
quick.how: It is applied as a lotion, mousse or spray in self-tanners, typically blended with DHA, and the colour develops over several hours. Users reapply as the tan fades over days to build or maintain colour.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed contain no safety or regulatory data specific to erythrulose.

angle.text: Erythrulose is a sugar used with DHA in self-tanners to give a sunless bronzed colour that appears within hours, by reacting with the outer skin layer. It is described as developing more slowly and fading more evenly; independent trials were not found.

silymarin-milk-thistle.summary: A milk thistle extract sold for liver support whose antioxidant chemistry has led people to try it for clearer, healthier-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Silymarin is the active extract of milk thistle, mainly sold as a liver-support supplement. People who take it for looks hope its antioxidant activity gives clearer, healthier-looking skin and slower visible ageing.

It is described as scavenging free radicals and chelating metals, with anti-inflammatory effects, and proposed skin benefits include protection from UV damage and inflammation. No human trials for skin or cosmetic outcomes were found.
quick.how: It is taken as a standardised capsule or tablet supplement, usually daily and over a long period. People pair it with ordinary skincare and sun protection rather than using it alone.
quick.risks: It may inhibit drug-metabolising enzymes and transporters, so interactions with medicines cannot be excluded; pregnancy data are limited.

angle.text: Silymarin is a milk thistle liver supplement that some people take for its antioxidant chemistry, hoping for clearer skin or slower visible ageing. The skin role is proposed; no human skin trials were found.

vilon.summary: A Lys-Glu dipeptide from Russian gerontology research, discussed in longevity circles as an anti-aging candidate; studied in cells and mice.

quick.overview:
Vilon is a two-amino-acid peptide (lysine and glutamic acid) developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in St. Petersburg and described as an immune-system and anti-aging "bioregulator". People discuss it in longevity circles, with a looks payoff that is the hope of slower tissue ageing and a younger appearance.

Khavinson's group proposes that Vilon loosens condensed chromatin in ageing lymphocytes and so reactivates silenced genes, reported from cell cultures. Published work is mostly cell-culture and mouse experiments, including effects on tumour development and lifespan in mice, much of it from the originating institute. No controlled human trial of Vilon was found and no appearance effect is established.
quick.how: It is sold as a research peptide and discussed in short-course bioregulator routines in longevity communities. Any visible effect on appearance is a hope rather than a documented result.
quick.risks: No systematic human safety data were found. It is not an approved drug in the US or EU and is sold as a research peptide.

angle.text: Vilon is a Lys-Glu peptide from Khavinson's bioregulator program, discussed as an anti-aging candidate on the idea that it slows tissue ageing and so a younger look. Data come from cell and mouse studies; no human trials are known.

pinealon.summary: A Glu-Asp-Arg tripeptide from Khavinson's lab marketed for brain and anti-aging use, with a looks link through sleep and healthy aging.

quick.overview:
Pinealon is a three-amino-acid peptide (glutamic acid, aspartic acid, arginine) developed in Russia as a brain-focused "bioregulator". It is promoted for neuroprotection and anti-aging, and its looks angle is better sleep, cognition and healthier aging.

Lab studies report that pinealon reduces reactive-oxygen-species build-up in cultured neurons and other cells and modulates signalling such as ERK 1/2, and labelled short peptides were reported to enter the cell nucleus and bind DNA in vitro. Published work is mostly cell cultures and rats, such as protection of rat offspring from prenatal hyperhomocysteinemia; a few Russian-language reports involve human groups.
quick.how: It is sold as a research peptide and used in nootropic and longevity routines, often in short courses. Effects people look for are subjective, such as sleep and mental clarity.
quick.risks: No systematic safety data are available. It is not an approved medicine and is sold as a research peptide.

angle.text: Pinealon is a short peptide marketed for brain and anti-aging use, with a looks angle through better sleep and healthier aging. Evidence is cell and rat data plus small Russian-language human reports.

thymogen.summary: A Glu-Trp dipeptide immunomodulator from Russian peptide research, discussed in longevity circles for immune and anti-aging claims.

quick.overview:
Thymogen is the brand name of a synthetic dipeptide, glutamyl-tryptophan, isolated from the calf thymus preparation Thymalin and then made synthetically. It is described as an immune system modulator, and people discuss it in longevity circles hoping for better immune resilience and healthier aging.

It is reported to activate T-cell differentiation, alter intracellular cyclic nucleotides and activate neutrophil chemotaxis, and it has been grouped among interferon-inducing immunomodulators developed in former socialist countries. Research is mostly animal and cell work from Khavinson's group; one rat study reported slower ageing and fewer spontaneous tumours. No appearance use is documented.
quick.how: It is described in the literature as a pharmaceutical in its Russian lineage and is discussed in longevity communities in short courses. Any effect on looks is a hope tied to general health rather than a documented result.
quick.risks: No systematic safety data appear in the sources, and it is not approved in the US or EU.

angle.text: Thymogen is an immune-modulating dipeptide from Russian peptide research, discussed for healthier aging through better immune resilience. Evidence is mostly animal and cell data with thin human reports; no appearance use is documented.

bronchogen.summary: An Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu tetrapeptide from Khavinson's lab aimed at lung tissue, discussed as an organ-specific anti-aging peptide.

quick.overview:
Bronchogen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu) from Khavinson's bioregulator program, described as targeting bronchial and lung tissue. In longevity circles it is discussed for organ rejuvenation and healthier aging.

It is reported to stimulate differentiation markers in aged bronchial cell cultures and, in rats with an induced obstructive lung condition, to improve bronchial epithelium and reduce inflammation. A biophysical study reported it stabilises DNA against melting. Published studies are in rats and cell cultures; no human trial was found and no appearance use is documented.
quick.how: It is sold as a research peptide and discussed in short-course organ-bioregulator routines in longevity communities. Any effect is a hope tied to lung health and aging rather than to looks directly.
quick.risks: No human safety data are available. It is not an approved medicine.

angle.text: Bronchogen is a short peptide aimed at lung tissue, discussed in longevity circles as an organ-specific anti-aging peptide for healthier aging. Data are rat and cell studies only; no human trials and no appearance link are known.

cardiogen.summary: An Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg tetrapeptide from Khavinson's lab aimed at heart tissue, discussed in longevity circles as an anti-aging peptide.

quick.overview:
Cardiogen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg) from the Khavinson bioregulator program, described as acting on cardiovascular tissue. In longevity circles it is discussed for organ rejuvenation and healthier aging.

It is reported to stimulate proliferation in heart-tissue cultures, lower the pro-apoptotic protein p53 and interact with DNA and histones. In old rats it was reported to inhibit growth of a transplanted M-1 sarcoma. The literature is limited to organotypic cultures and rats; no human studies were found and no appearance use is documented.
quick.how: It is sold as a research peptide and discussed in short-course organ-bioregulator routines in longevity communities. Any effect is a hope tied to heart health and aging rather than to looks directly.
quick.risks: No human safety data exist, and it is not approved for therapeutic use.

angle.text: Cardiogen is a short peptide aimed at heart tissue, discussed in longevity circles as an anti-aging peptide for healthier aging. Data are sparse rat and cell studies with no human trials; no appearance link is known.
